projects.title: TUSA MX: operational reporting for Meta Ads
projects.summary: For a four-venue bar, I turned campaign follow-up into two comparable daily cuts. The documented work covers November 2024 to August 2025, with 135 cuts and about nine weekly campaigns.
projects.problem: There were no shared templates to compare spend, messages, tables at the venue, and on-site visitors across venues and times. Ad photos and videos also arrived outside Meta's requested format.
projects.action: I built and documented Google Sheets and Excel templates. I collected Meta Ads and on-site movement at 3 PM and 10 PM, compared all four venues, and sent each report to the company WhatsApp group.
projects.result: I maintained 135 cuts with the same fields and schedule. The period recorded 11,600 messages and 6,800 visitors, with about 86 messages and 51 visitors per report. Per-campaign detail stays internal.

technical.detail: Google Sheets and Excel templates bring together Meta Ads data and activity across the four venues at 3 PM and 10 PM.
technical.benefit: Keeps the 135 cuts comparable with the same fields and schedule.

projects.title: Notion → Google Calendar: due-date automation
projects.summary: For a university client, one date is entered in Notion and the flow reflects it in Google Calendar with a reminder one day ahead. Real use ran from April to August 2026, with 5-10 tasks per week.
projects.problem: The same date and context had to be copied and maintained in two systems. Repeated work made it easier to miss an update or a due date.
projects.action: I set up a one-way Google Apps Script flow. It queries Notion page by page (pagination means requesting records in blocks until all are covered), creates, updates, or removes all-day events, and writes back only the event identifier (ID), status, and sync date. It does not rewrite academic fields.
projects.result: The daily load went from 5-10 to 2-3 minutes because each date is entered once. No failures were observed during the use period; the flow paused between semesters, and the available code review is static with no active trigger demonstrated.

technical.detail: Google Apps Script queries Notion page by page and creates, updates, or removes all-day Google Calendar events.
technical.benefit: Lets each date be entered once instead of maintained in both systems.

technical.detail: The flow writes back only the event ID, status, and sync date; it does not rewrite academic fields.
technical.benefit: Keeps academic fields unchanged during sync.

evidence.caption: Text evidence traced to the case and its checked structure; PDF visuals are withheld to protect the academic context.
evidence.provenance: Real use with a university client and a field structure checked live. The canonical PDF is not published because it may identify the context; the code and manifest are available as static backup.

projects.title: DLRO Editor: batch electrical reports
projects.summary: This offline Windows application replaces PDF-by-PDF correction with one guided session. In the documented real batch, 110 reports across two boxes and two amperage families pass through the workflow without editing the originals.
projects.problem: The manual process left values blank, misplaced the Comments block, lost symbols, and could flatten the box structure. Everything had to run without a network or server.
projects.action: I automated zone-based editing (each field is rewritten only inside its own box) on temporary copies, kept the review result by result for electrical safety, and added eight tabs, a per-row preview, and a ZIP export with integrity checks before and after.
projects.result: Regressions E1-E4 (the four automated tests for known errors) are covered. The documented run had 238 approved checks and 2 skipped; the ZIP is checked as a whole and originals remain untouched. The EXE was verified on the work machine, with no multi-machine rollout demonstrated.

technical.detail: Each field is rewritten only inside its own box and on temporary copies.
The workflow provides eight tabs, a per-row preview, and ZIP export with checks before and after.
technical.benefit: Supports result-by-result review and whole-ZIP verification.

evidence.caption: Text evidence traced to the 110-PDF case; client-PDF visuals are not published.
evidence.provenance: Real use with a 110-PDF batch. The canonical PDF is not published because it may identify the client; backup includes automated tests and read-only references with preserved integrity.

projects.title: Los Hornitos Uploader: locally controlled files
projects.summary: For this personal project, I built a file-sharing platform for a private community without depending on outside services. Documented use covered 8 or 9 people from March 26 to July 16, 2026, within an expectation of 10-12.
projects.problem: The previous sharing flow left open questions about storage, links, upload resumption, metadata recovery, and personal-data exposure.
projects.action: I built a local web app with a Windows launcher and HTTPS gateway. It stores files and metadata locally (binaries are the raw files), splits uploads into chunks, checks SHA-256 (a fingerprint that detects whether a file changed), creates single links and QR codes, and supports HTTP range downloads (resuming where they stopped).
projects.result: The community moved from outside services to owner-controlled storage, direct links, and local recovery. The Stable 0.5.1 installer was verified on the work machine. No measured speed, permanent availability, or off-machine backup is claimed.

technical.detail: The app splits uploads into chunks and checks the file's SHA-256 fingerprint.
technical.benefit: The fingerprint can detect whether a file changed.

technical.detail: The app creates individual links and QR codes and supports HTTP range downloads.
technical.benefit: A download can resume from where it was interrupted.

evidence.provenance: Own project used with a private community. The canonical PDF is not published because it contains personal data; code, tests, installer, and architecture notes remain in internal backup.

projects.title: Windows and ProtonVPN: DNS troubleshooting
projects.summary: This personal technical sample documents a Windows 10 name-resolution failure. The adapter remained connected and ping worked, but browsers and applications could not resolve domains.
projects.problem: IP connectivity and DNS resolution were being treated as the same problem. The original evidence does not include a browser-failure or Event Viewer screenshot, so those views remain labeled as recreated or conceptual.
projects.action: I separated IP connectivity from name resolution, linked the failure to a persistent ProtonVPN policy in the DnsPolicyConfig store, documented its removal, and flushed the resolver cache.
projects.result: The documented verification records an nslookup google.com response from dns.google at 8.8.8.8. Disabling ProtonVPN auto-connect was part of the described prevention; this is not presented as a universal fix.

technical.detail: The adapter remained connected and ping worked, but browsers and apps could not resolve domains.
technical.benefit: Separates name-resolution failure from IP connectivity.

technical.detail: The recorded check shows nslookup google.com answered by dns.google at 8.8.8.8; the documented intervention removed the persistent ProtonVPN policy and cleared the cache.
technical.benefit: Confirms resolution in this documented case without presenting it as a universal fix.

evidence.caption: Cover of the technical DNS case presentation; labels distinguish source evidence from recreated views.
evidence.provenance: Independent personal technical sample, not a paid-client testimonial. Only exports without local paths or personal identifiers were kept.

working.title: How I work
paragraphs: I start by clarifying what must change and what must stay untouched. Then I document the flow, its limits, and the evidence available.
I prefer steps that can be checked: sourced data, tests for changes, and an explanation that separates what is demonstrated from what remains open.
